newsitem.title: USA: Close scrutiny seen for any Delta-Continental pact.
newsitem.headline: Close scrutiny seen for any Delta-Continental pact.

text.p: Experts said Wednesday the U.S. government would closely scrutinize any merger between Continental Airlines and Delta Air Lines, in part because it would raise anti-trust questions at two major East Coast airports.

Published reports said Delta and Continental, which have extensive domestic and international routes, have held talks on a merger to create the world's largest airline. The carriers themselves have declined comment.
Don Farmer, a Washington anti-trust lawyer experienced in airline mergers, said the Justice Department would likely be most concerned about airports with restricted landing slots.

"The ones that are of the most anti-trust concern are the airports where no one else can get in, like New York and Washington," Farmer said. A consultant said a new combined airline would have a powerful position in those two cities.

Lawrence Crawford, president of the consulting firm of Avitas Aviation Inc, said the new comined airline would become the number one carrier at both National Airport in Washington and La Guardia Airport in New York.
"Those are two of the nation's four (landing) slot-restricted airports," he said. "The others are O'Hare in Chicago and Kennedy in New York. And Kennedy is mostly international."
The combined airline would also become the top carrier in Newark, N.J., and Boston, Crawford said. And it would be the top carrier in all cities in Florida except Miami, where it would be number two.

"That could have an effect on domestic competition in the East where fares have always tended to be higher and there has always been less competition," said a government aviation analyst, who asked not to be identified. "This may trigger a round of consolidation and Justice and the Department of Transportation will have to consider that."
But Rich Golaszewski of GRA Inc, an aviation research firm in Jenkintown, Pa., said he believed none of that would stop a merger.
"Is big itself bad?" he asked, noting that the government had permitted large railroad mergers to go ahead. "That becomes a value judgment."
Malcolm Pfunder, a Washington anti-trust lawyer, said that if the government does have a problem the airlines may have to respond by divesting themselves of some properties.
The review of any domestic aspects of a merger would be conducted by the Justice Department, while the foreign aspects will be reviewed by the Department of Transportation.

Asked about the possibility of a merger, Justice Department spokeswoman Gina Talamona said: "We're aware of it and it's something that we would take a look at, if it gets to the point where there's some kind of transaction."
